\section{Continuity}
A function $f: X \to Y$ is continuous at $a$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$
there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $x \in \ball{a}{\delta}$ implies
$\abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon$.

\begin{theorem}
If $f$ is continuous on a compact set $K$, then $f$ is uniformly
continuous on $K$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose not. Then for some $\varepsilon_0 > 0$ and every $n$ there are points
$x_n, y_n \in K$ with $d(x_n, y_n) < 1/n$ but
$\abs{f(x_n) - f(y_n)} \ge \varepsilon_0$.
Compactness gives a convergent subsequence of $\seq{x_n}$, and the
triangle inequality forces $\seq{y_n}$ to the same limit, contradicting
the bound on $\abs{f(x_n) - f(y_n)}$.
\end{proof}

The same argument with $\norm{\,\cdot\,}$ in place of the metric shows
that any continuous linear map between normed spaces is bounded.
